# Polymorphic Arrays
<!-- Slide 27 -->

## An Array of Parent Pointers {.smaller}

- A `Hash*` can point at a Toy, a SHA256, or a SHA3, and nothing is sliced.
- Will each object finally display itself?

::: notes
Slides 28–33

Students should expect yes. That expectation is the point of this topic.
:::

<!-- Slide 28 -->

---

## An Array of Parent Pointers

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {style="font-size: 55%;"}
~~~cpp
int main() {
  Hash* myToys[4];
  myToys[0] = new Hash("Hello World");
  myToys[1] = new Toy("Semper Fi");
  myToys[2] = new SHA256(
    "The happiness of your life depends upon the quality of your thoughts.");
  myToys[3] = new SHA3("Done!");


  for (auto h : myToys) h->Display();    // remember to change me

return 0;
}
~~~
:::
:::

::: {.column width="42%" style="font-size: 50%;"}
. . .

~~~
Base text: Hello World
Base text: Semper Fi
Base text: The happiness of your life
depends upon the quality of your
thoughts.
Base text: Done!
~~~
:::

::::

::: notes
Each object is built whole on the heap with new, and the array holds only addresses, so nothing is sliced. The loop uses -> because h is a pointer.

This program never deletes the four objects. Deleting through a Hash* correctly needs a virtual destructor, which is in 14.01.

Full program: cpp/hash_pointer_array.cpp
:::

<!-- Slide 30 -->

---

## Still Not Working

- No!
- It still isn't working!
- Why?

. . .

- In C++, polymorphism is turned **off** by DEFAULT.

::: notes
The objects are intact. Every Toy is still a whole Toy on the heap. The problem is which function the compiler chooses, which is the next slide.
:::

<!-- Slide 31 -->

---

## The Compiler Only Sees the Type

~~~cpp
Hash* h = myToys[1];   // points at a Toy
h->Display();          // the compiler sees Hash*, so it calls Hash::Display()
~~~

- The function is chosen when the program is compiled, from the pointer's type. The compiler never looks at the object. This is called static binding.
- Thursday's question gets the same answer: a `Person*` pointing at `ava` calls Person's `print()`.

::: notes
At compile time the compiler does not know what myToys[1] will point at; it only knows the pointer is a Hash*. So it picks Hash::Display() and builds that call into the program.

To get Toy::Display(), the choice has to wait until the program runs and can look at the object. That is what virtual turns on, in Topic 4.
:::

<!-- Slide 32 -->

---

## Summary

- An array of parent pointers holds every kind of child without slicing.
- Without `virtual`, the pointer's type picks the function at compile time, so every element still runs the parent's version.

::: notes

:::
